Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Test

Source: R/icc_test.R
icc_test.Rd

Estimates one intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), with a confidence interval and a test against a null value, and returns an object of class "htest". The ICC form is chosen with model, type and unit, following McGraw and Wong (1996).

Usage

icc_test(
  x = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  measure = NULL,
  item = NULL,
  id = NULL,
  col.names = NULL,
  model = c("twoway", "oneway"),
  type = c("consistency", "agreement"),
  unit = c("single", "average"),
  method = c("anova", "reml"),
  conf.level = 0.95,
  null.value = NULL,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "greater", "less"),
  boot = FALSE,
  boot_ci = c("auto", "perc", "bca", "stud", "basic"),
  replicates = 1999,
  se_method = c("jackknife", "influence", "normal")
)

Arguments

x

A formula of the form values ~ item | id, where values is the measurement, item identifies the trial, rater or occasion, and id identifies the subject. Use either x, the measure/item/id arguments, or col.names.

data

A data frame containing the variables.

measure, item, id

Column names (character) of the measurement, the item (trial, rater, or occasion) and the subject identifier, for data in long format.

col.names

Column names (character) of the items, for data in wide format (one row per subject).

model

"twoway" (default) when every subject is measured on the same set of items (e.g. test-retest trials), or "oneway" when each subject is measured by a different set of items (e.g. different raters).

type

"consistency" (default) excludes systematic differences between items from the ICC; "agreement" includes them (absolute agreement). Only "agreement" is defined for model = "oneway".

unit

"single" (default) for the reliability of a single measurement, or "average" for the reliability of the mean of all k items.

method

"anova" (default) estimates the variance components from the analysis of variance and requires complete, balanced data. "reml" fits a linear mixed model and allows missing measurements.

conf.level

Confidence level of the interval (default 0.95).

null.value

The ICC under the null hypothesis. The default, NULL, gives the estimate and interval without a test.

alternative

"two.sided" (default), "greater", or "less". Used only when null.value is given (without a test the interval is two-sided). A one-sided alternative gives a one-sided interval (see Details).

boot

If TRUE, use a nonparametric bootstrap that resamples subjects for the interval and p-value. Default FALSE.

boot_ci

Bootstrap interval type: "auto" (default), "perc" (percentile), "bca", "stud" (studentized), or "basic". "auto" uses "stud" for method = "anova" and "perc" for method = "reml" (and "perc" when se_method = "normal"); see Details. Used only when boot = TRUE.

replicates

Number of bootstrap replicates (default 1999).

se_method

How the standard error is estimated: "jackknife" (default; delete one subject at a time), "influence" (per-subject influence, or sandwich, estimate), or "normal" (normal theory). The SE is reported in stderr and is used by the studentized bootstrap; it does not change the F-based interval or test. See Details.

Value

A list of class c("reli_htest", "htest") containing:

statistic

The F statistic (omitted for bootstrap results).

parameter

The numerator and denominator degrees of freedom (omitted for bootstrap results).

p.value

The p-value of the test.

conf.int

The confidence interval for the ICC.

estimate

The estimated ICC, named by its McGraw and Wong form.

stderr

Standard errors of the ICC (ICC) and of \(z = 0.5 \log F\) (z), from se_method. With boot = TRUE, also boot: the standard deviation of the bootstrap ICC estimates.

null.value

The hypothesized ICC.

alternative

The alternative hypothesis.

method

A description of the ICC and the inference.

data.name

A description of the data.

fit

The fitted variance components, mean squares and model.

data

The data in long format.

settings

The settings used, for the methods.

boot

Bootstrap details (NULL unless boot = TRUE).

Details

ICC forms. McGraw and Wong (1996) and Shrout and Fleiss (1979) name the forms differently:

modeltypeunitMcGraw & WongShrout & Fleiss
onewayagreementsingleICC(1)ICC(1,1)
onewayagreementaverageICC(k)ICC(1,k)
twowayagreementsingleICC(A,1)ICC(2,1)
twowayagreementaverageICC(A,k)ICC(2,k)
twowayconsistencysingleICC(C,1)ICC(3,1)
twowayconsistencyaverageICC(C,k)ICC(3,k)

Whether items are treated as random or fixed changes the interpretation but not the calculation (McGraw & Wong, 1996). Average-measure forms are not defined for McGraw and Wong's two-way mixed model with an interaction.

Choosing the form. Answer three questions in order: (1) is every subject measured by the same items? Yes: "twoway"; no, each subject by different items: "oneway". (2) Should systematic differences between items count as error? Yes, when measurements from different items will be used interchangeably or on their absolute values (for example compared with a cut-off): "agreement"; no, when only the subjects' relative standing matters or systematic differences are reported separately: "consistency". (3) Will one measurement or the mean of the k items be used in practice? "single" or "average". The "Reliability Analysis" vignette has a table of common designs (vignette("reliability_analysis", package = "SimplyAgree")).

Related coefficients. With complete data, Cronbach's (1951) alpha equals ICC(C,k), the average-measure consistency ICC (McGraw & Wong, 1996): it describes the mean of the k items, not a single item. For two methods, Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (ccc_test()) is essentially ICC(A,1); the estimators differ only in using n rather than n - 1 in the variances (Nickerson, 1997; Carrasco & Jover, 2003).

Default form. The default, ICC(C,1), follows Hopkins (2000) and Weir (2005): check for systematic change between trials separately (for example with the trials F test, or t.test() for two trials), then report the consistency ICC, which is tied to the standard error of measurement (\(\sqrt{MS_E}\)). Others, such as Koo and Li (2016), recommend absolute agreement (type = "agreement") for test-retest studies. Which form is appropriate depends on whether systematic differences between trials should count as error.

Average-measure forms are computed as the Spearman-Brown projection of the single-measure form to all k items. With complete data this is identical to the McGraw and Wong formulas; with missing data it keeps the estimand the reliability of the mean of all k items.

Confidence intervals are the F-based intervals of Shrout and Fleiss (1979) and McGraw and Wong (1996, Table 7), with \(\alpha/2\) in each tail. They are exact for the one-way and consistency forms and approximate (Satterthwaite degrees of freedom) for the agreement forms. With alternative = "greater" the interval is one-sided, [L, 1], where L is the one-sided conf.level lower bound; with "less" it is [-Inf, U].

Tests. By default (null.value = NULL) no test is done: the result is the estimate and a two-sided interval. Testing against an ICC of 0, the default in many programs, is rarely informative for reliability. When null.value is given, the tests are the F tests of McGraw and Wong (1996, Table 8) of \(H_0: \rho = \rho_0\). They are exact for the one-way and consistency forms, and invert exactly to the interval. For the agreement forms the test and the interval are separate Satterthwaite approximations (degrees of freedom evaluated at \(\rho_0\) for the test and at the estimate for the interval), so with few subjects they can disagree near the interval limits; McGraw and Wong note that their power cannot be determined exactly.

Missing data. method = "reml" estimates the variance components from a linear mixed model and uses degrees of freedom based on the observed data (subject df \(n - 1\), error df \(N - n - k + 1\), with N the number of observations). The intervals and p-values are then approximate and a warning is given. In simulations with 20 subjects and 3 trials, 95% intervals covered 0.93 to 0.97 with 15% of measurements missing and 0.91 to 0.95 with 30% missing; coverage depends on the design and the pattern of missingness. boot = TRUE is an alternative.

Bootstrap. With boot = TRUE, subjects are resampled with replacement (keeping all of each subject's measurements) and the model is refitted. The BCa interval uses a leave-one-subject-out jackknife for the acceleration. The studentized interval works on the scale \(z = 0.5 \log F\) and divides each replicate by its own standard error from se_method; a normal-theory SE cannot be used because it depends only on the degrees of freedom, which would reduce the studentized interval to the basic interval on the z scale. The p-value is obtained by inverting the chosen interval (as in the TOSTER package), so it is approximate and consistent with the interval. With method = "reml" each replicate refits the mixed model, which can be slow.

For the two-way agreement forms, resampling subjects alone would treat the items as fixed and ignore the uncertainty from sampling the items, which under-covered badly in simulations (0.70 to 0.80 with an ICC of 0.9). Each replicate therefore also multiplies the item mean square by an independent \(\chi^2_{k-1}/(k-1)\) draw, its normal-theory sampling variation (a hybrid bootstrap developed for this package). Like the F interval, this treats the items as a random sample; when the items are fixed it is conservative.

The bootstrap is mainly useful when the data are clearly non-normal. In simulations (3 trials, 10 or 30 subjects, ICC 0.5 or 0.9), the F intervals covered about 0.92 to 0.97 with normal, complete data but only 0.80 to 0.93 with skewed or heavy-tailed data. With complete data, the studentized bootstrap with the jackknife SE covered 0.90 to 0.965 for the consistency ICC, including 0.94 to 0.955 with skewed data and 30 subjects, and was the best method overall; for the agreement ICC it was roughly tied with the percentile interval (0.89 to 0.955), whose lower bound was too high less often. With 20% of measurements missing and method = "reml", the studentized interval (which then needs the influence SE) was unreliable at moderate ICCs (as low as 0.80), while the percentile interval covered 0.87 to 0.96. Hence boot_ci = "auto", and a warning when "stud" is requested with method = "reml". BCa never improved on the percentile interval. Every method under-covered with 10 subjects, skewed data and an ICC of 0.9 (0.84 to 0.91).

Standard errors. stderr gives the standard error of \(z = 0.5 \log F\) (the scale of the studentized bootstrap) and, by the delta method, of the ICC. The jackknife (default) deletes one subject at a time; with complete data it uses closed-form leave-one-out mean squares, and with method = "reml" it refits the model n times. The influence estimate is a sandwich estimate from each subject's influence on the mean squares (with missing data, an approximation from each subject's observed measurements); it is cheaper but too small with few subjects. The normal-theory SE depends only on the degrees of freedom. In simulations (3 trials, 20 to 40 subjects, up to 30% missing), the jackknife SE averaged 0.89 to 1.08 times the true sampling SD, the influence SE 0.69 to 1.00 (lowest with few subjects, skewed data, or data missing at random), and the normal-theory SE 0.87 to 1.04 with normal data but 0.60 to 0.80 with skewed or heavy-tailed data. For the agreement forms, the jackknife and influence SEs add the normal-theory variance of the item mean square, treating the items as random. The studentized bootstrap needs an SE estimated from each resample, so it cannot use "normal"; with method = "reml" it requires "influence", because the jackknife would refit the model n times in every replicate.

Interpreting the ICC. No qualitative labels (such as "good" or "excellent") are given: published cutoffs disagree, and the ICC depends on how much subjects differ from each other (Weir, 2005). To claim that reliability exceeds a threshold, test against it, e.g. null.value = 0.75, alternative = "greater".

References

Carrasco, J. L., & Jover, L. (2003). Estimating the generalized concordance correlation coefficient through variance components. Biometrics, 59(4), 849-858. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341x.2003.00099.x

Cronbach, L. J. (1951). Coefficient alpha and the internal structure of tests. Psychometrika, 16(3), 297-334. doi:10.1007/BF02310555

Hopkins, W. G. (2000). Measures of reliability in sports medicine and science. Sports Medicine, 30(1), 1-15. doi:10.2165/00007256-200030010-00001

Koo, T. K., & Li, M. Y. (2016). A guideline of selecting and reporting intraclass correlation coefficients for reliability research. Journal of Chiropractic Medicine, 15(2), 155-163. doi:10.1016/j.jcm.2016.02.012

McGraw, K. O., & Wong, S. P. (1996). Forming inferences about some intraclass correlation coefficients. Psychological Methods, 1(1), 30-46. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.1.1.30

Nickerson, C. A. E. (1997). A note on "A concordance correlation coefficient to evaluate reproducibility". Biometrics, 53(4), 1503-1507. doi:10.2307/2533516

Shrout, P. E., & Fleiss, J. L. (1979). Intraclass correlations: Uses in assessing rater reliability. Psychological Bulletin, 86(2), 420-428. doi:10.1037/0033-2909.86.2.420

Ukoumunne, O. C., Davison, A. C., Gulliford, M. C., & Chinn, S. (2003). Non-parametric bootstrap confidence intervals for the intraclass correlation coefficient. Statistics in Medicine, 22(24), 3805-3821. doi:10.1002/sim.1643

Weir, J. P. (2005). Quantifying test-retest reliability using the intraclass correlation coefficient and the SEM. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 19(1), 231-240. doi:10.1519/15184.1

See also

reli_htest-methods for summary(), plot() and check().

Examples

# Shrout & Fleiss (1979) example: 6 subjects rated by 4 judges
sf <- data.frame(J1 = c(9, 6, 8, 7, 10, 6), J2 = c(2, 1, 4, 1, 5, 2),
                 J3 = c(5, 3, 6, 2, 6, 4), J4 = c(8, 2, 8, 6, 9, 7))
icc_test(col.names = c("J1", "J2", "J3", "J4"), data = sf)
#> 
#> 	Two-way, consistency, single-measure ICC [Shrout & Fleiss ICC(3,1)]
#> 
#> data:  J1, J2, J3, J4
#> 
#> alternative hypothesis: two.sided
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  0.3424648 0.9458583
#> sample estimates:
#>  ICC(C,1) 
#> 0.7148407 
#> 

# Absolute agreement, tested against 0.5
icc_test(col.names = c("J1", "J2", "J3", "J4"), data = sf,
         type = "agreement", null.value = 0.5, alternative = "greater")
#> 
#> 	Two-way, absolute agreement, single-measure ICC [Shrout & Fleiss
#> 	ICC(2,1)]
#> 
#> data:  J1, J2, J3, J4
#> F = 0.43113, df1 = 5.0000, df2 = 4.3128, p-value = 0.8101
#> alternative hypothesis: true ICC is greater than 0.5
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  0.04290119 1.00000000
#> sample estimates:
#>  ICC(A,1) 
#> 0.2897638 
#> 

# Long data with a formula
sf_long <- data.frame(id = rep(1:6, times = 4),
                      judge = rep(c("J1", "J2", "J3", "J4"), each = 6),
                      score = c(sf$J1, sf$J2, sf$J3, sf$J4))
res <- icc_test(score ~ judge | id, data = sf_long)
summary(res)
#> The estimated ICC(C,1) was 0.715 (95% compatibility interval [0.342,
#> 0.946]). Values in this interval are the most compatible with the data,
#> given the model and its assumptions. The estimate is the two-way,
#> consistency, single-measure ICC (McGraw & Wong ICC(C,1); Shrout &
#> Fleiss ICC(3,1)): the reliability of a single measurement, excluding
#> systematic differences between items. The data had 6 subjects and 4
#> items (24 measurements, none missing); variance components were
#> estimated by analysis of variance. The F-based interval is exact
#> (McGraw & Wong, 1996).
